title: Getting Started with momst
text: momst package solves Multi-Objective Minimum Spanning Tree (MO-MST) problem complete weighted graphs. Given graph every edge carries two three independent costs (example: distance, time, risk), goal obtain Pareto front spanning trees tree dominates objectives simultaneously. solver built around NSGA-II algorithm (Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II) uses Prufer sequences chromosome representation. Cayley’s theorem, every integer vector length n - 2 values {1, ..., n} decodes unique spanning tree n nodes, representation closed random sampling, crossover, mutation. avoids need repair operator. package exposes four solver variants differ local search operator applied generation: vignette shows minimal workflow: Generate random instance. Run run_momst() chosen variant. Inspect population, per-iteration Pareto fronts, global Pareto front. Visualise global Pareto front best-compromise spanning tree. companion vignette (vignette("momst-variants", package = "momst")) compares four variants side side.

what: Step 1. Generate a random bi-objective instance
title: Getting Started with momst
text: generate_instance() returns edge list complete graph random uniform weights every objective. seed argument makes instance fully reproducible without polluting global random number generator. performance, package converts edge list one n x n lookup matrix per objective cost edge (, j) can retrieved constant time:
code: # Number of nodes and number of objectives n_nodes   <- 10 n_obj     <- 2  # Generate a complete graph with two independent weights per edge inst <- generate_instance(   n        = n_nodes,   num_obj  = n_obj,   range_a  = c(10, 100),   # weight range for objective 1   range_b  = c(10,  50),   # weight range for objective 2   seed     = 12345 )  # The instance has n*(n-1)/2 edges nrow(inst) #> [1] 45  # First six edges of the complete graph head(inst) #>   from to weight_1 weight_2 #> 1    1  2 74.88135 22.84899 #> 2    1  3 88.81959 12.40781 #> 3    1  4 78.48841 11.73826 #> 4    1  5 89.75121 12.20215 #> 5    1  6 51.08329 35.02171 #> 6    1  7 24.97346 48.57881 lk <- build_weight_lookup(inst, n_nodes, n_obj)  # Each element is a symmetric weight matrix str(lk, max.level = 1) #> List of 2 #>  $ : num [1:10, 1:10] 0 74.9 88.8 78.5 89.8 ... #>  $ : num [1:10, 1:10] 0 22.8 12.4 11.7 12.2 ...  # Weight of edge (1, 2) in objective 1 lk[[1]][1, 2] #> [1] 74.88135

what: Step 2. Run the NSGA-II solver (base variant)
title: Getting Started with momst
text: run_momst() main entry point. performs: iterations independent runs NSGA-II (useful average results). Inside run, max_generations evolutionary cycles. every cycle, local search operator applied current non-dominated set (none "base"). global Pareto front assembled final population independent run. first contact use simplest variant, "base". small instance short runs enough illustrate workflow. function returns list everything needed analyse results: instance : edge list used. lookup : per-objective weight matrices. iterations : final populations every independent run. pareto_per_iter : Pareto front every independent run. global_pareto : non-dominated union fronts. elapsed : wall-clock time seconds.
code: res_base <- run_momst(   instance        = inst,   n               = n_nodes,   num_obj         = n_obj,   variant         = "base",      # pure NSGA-II   iterations      = 3,           # three independent runs   pop_size        = 30,          # must be even   tour_size       = 2,           # binary tournament selection   cross_rate      = 0.80,        # crossover probability   mut_rate        = 0.10,        # per-individual mutation probability   max_generations = 40,          # generations per run   convergence_window = 8,        # early stopping window   verbose         = FALSE,   seed            = 2026 ) names(res_base) #> [1] "instance"        "lookup"          "iterations"      "pareto_per_iter" #> [5] "global_pareto"   "elapsed"

what: Step 3. Inspect the global Pareto front
title: Getting Started with momst
text: row global_pareto candidate spanning tree. first n - 2 columns Prufer sequence (chromosome), columns objective_1, objective_2 (optionally objective_3) report total cost tree objective. can sort front objective 1 see typical trade-objectives: “extreme” solutions front trees minimise objective isolation:

title: Getting Started with momst

title: Getting Started with momst
text: workflow extends seamlessly three-objective problems. Just set num_obj = 3 supply third weight range range_c. Pareto front lives three-dimensional objective space. simple way inspect three-objective front without extra dependencies pairs plot: Pairwise projections three-objective Pareto front.
code: res_3obj <- run_momst(   n               = 8,   num_obj         = 3,   variant         = "base",   iterations      = 2,   pop_size        = 30,   max_generations = 25,   range_a         = c(10, 100),   range_b         = c(10,  50),   range_c         = c(30, 200),   verbose         = FALSE,   seed            = 7 )  # Three-objective non-dominated set head(res_3obj$global_pareto[, c("objective_1", "objective_2", "objective_3")]) #>       objective_1 objective_2 objective_3 #> X.10     377.2130    105.1852    672.9824 #> X.221    421.0996    114.1803    623.2404 #> X.101    229.8941    155.1778    732.7992 #> X.131    389.0804    189.9002    350.9168 #> X.3      290.4036    204.5720    478.7301 #> X.5      256.0040    135.4129    823.3894 front3 <- res_3obj$global_pareto[, c("objective_1", "objective_2", "objective_3")] pairs(front3, pch = 19, col = "steelblue")

title: Getting Started with momst

code: a <- run_momst(n = 8, num_obj = 2, variant = "base",                iterations = 1, pop_size = 20, max_generations = 15,                verbose = FALSE, seed = 99)  b <- run_momst(n = 8, num_obj = 2, variant = "base",                iterations = 1, pop_size = 20, max_generations = 15,                verbose = FALSE, seed = 99)  identical(a$global_pareto, b$global_pareto) #> [1] TRUE

title: Comparing the Four MO-MST Variants
text: instance, population size, seed fixed four variants start identical state. small wrapper makes per-variant call shorter:
code: # Problem size and number of objectives n_nodes <- 12 n_obj   <- 2  # A single instance reused by all variants shared_instance <- generate_instance(   n        = n_nodes,   num_obj  = n_obj,   range_a  = c(10, 100),   range_b  = c(10,  50),   seed     = 2026 )  # NSGA-II hyper-parameters shared by every run common_args <- list(   instance           = shared_instance,   n                  = n_nodes,   num_obj            = n_obj,   iterations         = 3,        # three independent runs per variant   pop_size           = 40,   tour_size          = 2,   cross_rate         = 0.80,   mut_rate           = 0.10,   max_generations    = 50,   convergence_window = 10,   verbose            = FALSE,   seed               = 123 ) # Run a given variant with the common arguments. run_variant <- function(variant) {   do.call(run_momst, c(common_args, list(variant = variant))) }

title: Comparing the Four MO-MST Variants
text: result list structure described Getting Started vignette. particularly interested global_pareto, non-dominated union fronts obtained across independent runs.
code: # Pure NSGA-II without local search res_base <- run_variant("base")  # NSGA-II + Path Relinking res_PR   <- run_variant("PR")  # NSGA-II + Pareto Local Search res_PLS  <- run_variant("PLS")  # NSGA-II + Tabu Search res_TS   <- run_variant("TS")

title: Comparing the Four MO-MST Variants
text: every variant collect objective values every solution global Pareto front: quick numerical summary front: columns mean: n_solutions : many non-dominated trees variant returns. best_obj1 : minimum value objective 1 found across front. best_obj2 : minimum value objective 2 found across front. mean_obj1 : average value objective 1 front (rough proxy “centre mass” front along axis). mean_obj2 : , objective 2. Note solutions automatically mean better quality: front well-spread points can dominate front many crowded points.
code: # Helper: extract just the objective columns from the global Pareto front extract_obj <- function(res, label) {   front <- res$global_pareto   data.frame(     variant    = label,     objective_1 = front$objective_1,     objective_2 = front$objective_2   ) }  fronts_all <- rbind(   extract_obj(res_base, "base"),   extract_obj(res_PR,   "PR"),   extract_obj(res_PLS,  "PLS"),   extract_obj(res_TS,   "TS") )  # Number of non-dominated solutions returned by each variant table(fronts_all$variant) #>  #> base  PLS   PR   TS  #>   16   30   34   23 # Best value reached per objective and number of non-dominated points summary_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(   split(fronts_all, fronts_all$variant),   function(df) {     data.frame(       variant     = unique(df$variant),       n_solutions = nrow(df),       best_obj1   = round(min(df$objective_1), 2),       best_obj2   = round(min(df$objective_2), 2),       mean_obj1   = round(mean(df$objective_1), 2),       mean_obj2   = round(mean(df$objective_2), 2)     )   } )) rownames(summary_table) <- NULL summary_table #>   variant n_solutions best_obj1 best_obj2 mean_obj1 mean_obj2 #> 1    base          16    215.91    181.99    321.10    230.38 #> 2     PLS          30    198.51    183.98    334.27    219.51 #> 3      PR          34    192.77    186.89    303.85    257.03 #> 4      TS          23    183.78    184.75    270.31    262.22

code: # Colour palette: one distinct colour per variant palette_var <- c(base = "#1f77b4",                  PR   = "#d62728",                  PLS  = "#2ca02c",                  TS   = "#9467bd")  # Set plotting limits from the union of all fronts xlim <- range(fronts_all$objective_1) ylim <- range(fronts_all$objective_2)  plot(NA, NA, xlim = xlim, ylim = ylim,      xlab = "Objective 1", ylab = "Objective 2",      main = "Pareto fronts: base vs PR vs PLS vs TS")  # Draw each variant in its colour, connecting the points with a dashed line for (v in names(palette_var)) {   sub <- fronts_all[fronts_all$variant == v, ]   sub <- sub[order(sub$objective_1), ]   lines(sub$objective_1, sub$objective_2,         col = palette_var[v], lty = 2, lwd = 1.2)   points(sub$objective_1, sub$objective_2,          col = palette_var[v], pch = 19) }  legend("topright", legend = names(palette_var),        col = palette_var, pch = 19, lty = 2, bty = "n")

title: Comparing the Four MO-MST Variants
text: simple way evaluate quality every individual variant build combined Pareto front solutions returned four variants check variants contribute points . contribution column tells many trees returned variant remain non-dominated faced union variants. Variants whose contribution close total size combined_front producing front-quality solutions; variants low contribution return many solutions dominated trees found others. Combined Pareto front (black) top variant front.
code: # Pool every chromosome from every variant all_chr <- rbind(   res_base$global_pareto[, 1:(n_nodes - 2), drop = FALSE],   res_PR$global_pareto[,   1:(n_nodes - 2), drop = FALSE],   res_PLS$global_pareto[,  1:(n_nodes - 2), drop = FALSE],   res_TS$global_pareto[,   1:(n_nodes - 2), drop = FALSE] ) all_chr <- unique(as.matrix(all_chr))  # Evaluate the pooled set on the shared instance ev <- compute_objectives(shared_instance, all_chr, n_obj,                          lookup = build_weight_lookup(shared_instance, n_nodes, n_obj))  # Keep only the non-dominated solutions of the pooled set ev <- non_dominated_crowding(ev, n_obj) combined_front <- as.data.frame(ev[ev[, "rankingIndex"] == 1, , drop = FALSE])  # How many trees define the combined Pareto front nrow(combined_front) #> [1] 30 # Build a key for each tree on the combined front key_combined <- apply(combined_front[, 1:(n_nodes - 2)], 1,                       function(r) paste(as.integer(r), collapse = "_"))  # Same key for the front of every variant key_of <- function(res) {   apply(res$global_pareto[, 1:(n_nodes - 2), drop = FALSE], 1,         function(r) paste(as.integer(r), collapse = "_")) }  # Number of solutions of each variant that survive on the combined front contribution <- data.frame(   variant      = c("base", "PR", "PLS", "TS"),   contribution = c(     sum(key_of(res_base) %in% key_combined),     sum(key_of(res_PR)   %in% key_combined),     sum(key_of(res_PLS)  %in% key_combined),     sum(key_of(res_TS)   %in% key_combined)   ) ) contribution #>   variant contribution #> 1    base            4 #> 2      PR            1 #> 3     PLS           18 #> 4      TS            7 plot(NA, NA, xlim = xlim, ylim = ylim,      xlab = "Objective 1", ylab = "Objective 2",      main = "Variants vs combined Pareto front")  for (v in names(palette_var)) {   sub <- fronts_all[fronts_all$variant == v, ]   sub <- sub[order(sub$objective_1), ]   points(sub$objective_1, sub$objective_2,          col = palette_var[v], pch = 1) }  cf <- combined_front[order(combined_front$objective_1), ] points(cf$objective_1, cf$objective_2,        col = "black", pch = 19, cex = 1.1) lines(cf$objective_1, cf$objective_2, col = "black", lwd = 1.4)  legend("topright",        legend = c("base", "PR", "PLS", "TS", "Combined"),        col    = c(palette_var, "black"),        pch    = c(rep(1, 4), 19),        lty    = c(rep(NA, 4), 1),        bty    = "n")

code: common_3 <- list(   n                  = 9,   num_obj            = 3,   iterations         = 2,   pop_size           = 30,   max_generations    = 30,   range_a            = c(10, 100),   range_b            = c(10,  50),   range_c            = c(30, 200),   convergence_window = 8,   verbose            = FALSE,   seed               = 555 )  run_variant_3 <- function(variant) {   do.call(run_momst, c(common_3, list(variant = variant))) }  res3_base <- run_variant_3("base") res3_PR   <- run_variant_3("PR") res3_PLS  <- run_variant_3("PLS") res3_TS   <- run_variant_3("TS") # Numerical summary across the three objectives summary_3 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(   list(base = res3_base, PR = res3_PR, PLS = res3_PLS, TS = res3_TS),   function(res) {     f <- res$global_pareto     c(n = nrow(f),       best_o1 = round(min(f$objective_1), 2),       best_o2 = round(min(f$objective_2), 2),       best_o3 = round(min(f$objective_3), 2))   } )) summary_3 #>       n best_o1 best_o2 best_o3 #> base 28  222.83  137.52  440.42 #> PR   33  201.97  129.99  413.48 #> PLS  37  203.56  129.64  376.79 #> TS   42  196.06  119.77  428.58 # Combine the three-objective fronts and project them pairwise df3 <- rbind(   data.frame(variant = "base", res3_base$global_pareto[, c("objective_1","objective_2","objective_3")]),   data.frame(variant = "PR",   res3_PR$global_pareto[,   c("objective_1","objective_2","objective_3")]),   data.frame(variant = "PLS",  res3_PLS$global_pareto[,  c("objective_1","objective_2","objective_3")]),   data.frame(variant = "TS",   res3_TS$global_pareto[,   c("objective_1","objective_2","objective_3")]) )  # Colour by variant col_v <- palette_var[df3$variant] pairs(df3[, c("objective_1", "objective_2", "objective_3")],       col = col_v, pch = 19,       main = "Three-objective Pareto fronts (colour by variant)")

what: momst: Multi-Objective Minimum Spanning Tree via NSGA-II with Local Search — momst-package
title: momst: Multi-Objective Minimum Spanning Tree via NSGA-II with Local Search — momst-package
text: momst package implements Multi-Criteria Minimum Spanning Tree (mc-MST) algorithm using NSGA-II (Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II). Four variants supported depending local search operator applied generation: "base" Pure NSGA-II without local search. "PR" NSGA-II plus Path Relinking. "PLS" NSGA-II plus Pareto Local Search. "TS" NSGA-II plus Tabu Search.

title: momst: Multi-Objective Minimum Spanning Tree via NSGA-II with Local Search — momst-package
text: Chromosomes encoded Prufer sequences, taking advantage Cayley's theorem (every sequence length n-2 values {1,...,n} decodes unique spanning tree n nodes). bijection makes every random chromosome valid solution, avoiding repair operators. main entry point run_momst.

title: momst: Multi-Objective Minimum Spanning Tree via NSGA-II with Local Search — momst-package
text: package reference implementation method described : Parraga-Alava, J., Inostroza-Ponta, M., & Dorn, M. (2017). Using local search strategies improve performance NSGA-II Multi-Criteria Minimum Spanning Tree problem. 2017 IEEE Congress Evolutionary Computation (CEC) (pp. 1818-1825). IEEE. doi:10.1109/CEC.2017.7969432

title: momst 0.1.0
text: Initial public release package. Reference implementation Parraga-Alava, Inostroza-Ponta Dorn (2017), “Using local search strategies improve performance NSGA-II Multi-Criteria Minimum Spanning Tree problem” (doi:10.1109/CEC.2017.7969432). Four solver variants exposed run_momst(): "base", "PR", "PLS", "TS". Support 2 3 objective formulations. Two vignettes: Getting Started momst Comparing Four MO-MST Variants.
